transcript:
This message comes from Schwab. At Schwab, you can get everything from self-directed investing to full-service wealth management, all in one place.
No matter your investing goal, life stage, amount to invest, or know-how, you can invest your way with Schwab.
This is NPR News Now. The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Dave Mattingly. Evacuations are underway along the Florida Panhandle as Hurricane Isaias gains strength in the Gulf.
The storm is expected to make landfall somewhere between southeastern Louisiana and the Florida Panhandle in the next 36 to 48 hours.
Residents and tourists are being told to leave in areas that include Fort Walton Beach and Destin, as NPR's Debbie Elliott reports.
National Hurricane Center Director Mike Brennan says Isaias is gaining steam as it moves over the warm waters of the Gulf of Mexico.
Isaias is expected to be a strengthening, strong hurricane as it approaches the northern Gulf Coast on Friday into Friday night and Saturday.
You can see multiple life-threatening impacts from storm surge, heavy rainfall flooding, and hurricane force winds.
The governors of Alabama and Florida have declared states of emergencies, and the impending storm has prompted school closures and event cancellations throughout the region.
The Marine Minerals Administration reports about 25 percent of offshore oil and 16 percent of natural gas production in the Gulf has been curtailed. Debbie Elliott, NPR News.
The hurricane's top sustained winds are currently 80 miles per hour. Less than a month before the November midterm elections, President Trump continues traveling to red states to campaign for Republican candidates.
He was in Texas last night where he rallied voters to support GOP Senate candidate Ken Paxton, the state's attorney general.
Mr. President, I want to thank you for coming for me, for coming for us, and for coming for Texas. We are going to win this race. God bless you.
Trump was repeatedly interrupted by protesters at the rally in San Antonio. Corporate executives in the U.S. are expressing growing concerns about artificial intelligence enabling fraud.
NPR's Jenna McLaughlin says those concerns are changing how those same executives invest to combat the threat.
According to the results of a survey of business leaders, over 80 percent said their company had already been targeted with AI-enabled scams, from convincing impersonations to deceptive fake business emails.
The research, first shared with NPR, was conducted by Sertos, a financial fraud intelligence firm that's part of a portfolio of businesses owned by seven of the largest financial institutions in the U.S.
Ben Chance, Sertos' manager, says businesses in the financial industry are on the front lines of new digital attacks.
This sector, you know, really, we have to be on our toes at all times, right? This is a, you know, a hot war, so to speak.
Around 80 percent of respondents said they worry AI scams could undermine trust in their business and in commerce writ large if safety isn't a priority.
Jenna McLaughlin, NPR News.
Wall Street futures are lower this morning. This is NPR News from Washington.
The French government says it will suspend the use of stun grenades in its policing of student protests in response to a 15-year-old's hand being blown off.
The devices are known as "sting ball grenades." They're used to disperse protesters when officers are surrounded and feel threatened.
The devices are banned in most European countries. NPR's Eleanor Beardsley reports on the latest protests there.
In a speech to the nation, Prime Minister Sebastien Le Corneux said contrary to what people are saying,
the police do not have orders to confront the students and are trying to use proportional force in a difficult context.
But there's been anger over what many say are overly aggressive police tactics.
Students and police faced off in Paris for several tense hours outside an elite university whose students have joined the high school movement.
The students chanted anti-police slogans from behind a barricade of trash bins until the police charged with tear gas to eventually clear the street.
Eleanor Beardsley in Pure News, Paris.
All 19 Federal Reserve policymakers were in agreement to raise interest rates by a quarter point at last month's meeting.
That's what minutes from the Fed meeting show they were released yesterday.
Inflation in the U.S. economy remains the Fed's top concern. It's above 3 percent, and the central bank's annual target is 2 percent.
Later this morning, the Labor Department reports on new claims for unemployment benefits in the U.S.
I'm Dave Mattingly, NPR News, in Washington.
